items.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
items.desc: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make metasurfaces strongly absorb UV light.

items.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
items.desc: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed. This sequesters a region needed by two effectors, the kinase CK2 and the ubiquitin ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which act sequentially to signal TDO2

items.title: New method measures microplastics in the air using an uncrewed aerial system
items.desc: Microplastics have been found in our bodies and the food we eat—and even in remote environments around the world, including seawater and ice in the Arctic. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how they move through the atmosphere. New CIRES-led research, which demonstrates a new method for sampling microplastics in the atmosphere using an uncrewed aerial system (UAS), aims to change that. The findings are published in the journal Scientific Reports.

items.title: Future warming events will outdo the extreme heat waves of the recent past, new study finds
items.desc: The extreme heat waves we have seen over the last few years may only serve as a preview of what is to come as a result of climate change. A new study led by researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner from Freie Universität Berlin, published in Nature Communications, finds that future heat waves could last longer, impact larger areas, and be much more severe.

items.title: Light-powered method resurrects 'dead-end' compounds for drug discovery
items.desc: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines. A Florida State University researcher is part of a team that has discovered a new way to give some of these "dead ends" a second chance at becoming the foundation for tomorrow's blockbuster drugs.

items.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
items.desc: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible. The study, published in Science, provides an important foundation for future quantum simulations of nuclear physics and materials science.

items.title: European forests need to solve two crises—but not necessarily in one place
items.desc: Forest areas can act both as carbon sinks and as vital habitats for thousands of species—but not necessarily at the same time. This has important implications for how Europe should manage its forests, says a University of Copenhagen researcher.

items.title: MTG-I2 satellite delivers remarkable first images, capturing a weather view of Europe every 2.5 minutes
items.desc: Europe's meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT, has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite's launch on Aug. 27, 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings.

items.title: High-precision timeline helps clarify an ancient magma surge in the North Cascades
items.desc: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal. However, what triggers these extreme surges, which last tens of millions of years, can be unclear.

items.title: AI won't ever make a historically accurate film—but it could help archaeology create better stories
items.desc: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer's "Odyssey" by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticized for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story "historically accurate and true to the art of Homer" at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.

items.title: AI points researchers toward new disease targets hidden in mitochondria
items.desc: Artificial intelligence is helping Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists fast-track answers to a long-standing question in human biology: What do hundreds of mystery proteins in the mitochondria actually do?

items.title: Redefining honesty in a crisis: Why truth alone is not enough
items.desc: When a company suffers a cyberattack, leaks customer data or faces a major public scandal, telling the truth is essential. But new research suggests it is not enough on its own: organizations also need to communicate early, treat people with respect and show how they intend to put things right.

items.title: 'Mega heat waves' strengthened by interaction between soil moisture, atmospheric pressure and temperature
items.desc: A new study has found that a self-reinforcing interaction between temperature, soil moisture and atmospheric pressure is being triggered at high temperatures, making extreme heat waves 10% hotter than they would otherwise be. The study was published in Science Advances and led by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA).

items.title: Fruit fly study offers clues to insect survival in a hotter, drier world
items.desc: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have identified a specialized lipid barrier in the fruit fly pupa that protects against dehydration in dry and hot environments. Their findings also expose the lipid barrier's limit, suggesting that insects in some regions of the world may struggle to adapt to climate change.

items.title: Beyond trial and error: A framework for AI-driven solid-electrolyte discovery
items.desc: A battery material can look perfect in the lab and still fail in a real battery. That is the puzzle facing researchers working on solid electrolytes, the materials seen as key to safer, longer-lasting batteries.

items.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
items.desc: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

items.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
items.desc: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
items.desc: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

items.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
items.desc: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

items.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
items.desc: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

items.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
items.desc: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

items.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
items.desc: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.

items.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
items.desc: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

items.title: Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
items.desc: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.

items.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
items.desc: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

items.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
items.desc: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
items.desc: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

items.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
items.desc: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

items.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
items.desc: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

items.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
items.desc: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

items.title: The Economic Toll of Israel’s Wars
items.desc: Israel’s economy may look strong, but three years of war have inflicted far greater damage than its robust stock market and appreciating currency suggest. Defense spending and government borrowing have risen sharply, while falling output and investment point to a prolonged recession.

items.title: Rebalancing Nature’s Books
items.desc: The first report card on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal framework was issued at this year’s UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, and the marks were dismal. The problem is not a lack of targets, but a global financial system that pays to destroy nature and penalizes those who protect it.

items.title: Only Israel’s Arab Parties Can Restore Its Democracy
items.desc: While Israel’s recent election did not deliver the transformation for which many might have hoped, it could open the way to restoring Israeli democracy. By building a coalition with the Arab-led parties, the opposition bloc could defeat not only Benjamin Netanyahu but also the violent, racist ideology he embodies.

items.title: Making the Most of America’s Midterm Tsunami
items.desc: American voters’ demand for the rule of law and democracy has helped destroy Trump’s MAGA movement. Affordability may have ranked first among their concerns, but addressing it will depend on repairing and improving democratic institutions.

items.title: AI Can Help Governments Help Citizens
items.desc: In developing economies, the AI debate has focused less on frontier risk and more on how to ensure that the technology actually serves people. That will require not only designing AI tools to work within government, but also investing in the state capacity required to put the technology to use.

items.title: MAGA’s Midterm Defeat Won’t Change the Course of History
items.desc: The world must not succumb to euphoria following Donald Trump’s latest defeat. If anything, his lame-duck status deprives Americans and everyone else of an excuse for avoiding hard conversations about the truly radical changes that will be needed to avert future catastrophes.

items.title: Can AI Colonialism Be Prevented?
items.desc: As the United States and China cement their technological dominance, the AI revolution threatens to reproduce the colonial dynamics of the first Industrial Revolution. To avoid digital colonization, middle powers must work together to build an open AI stack and establish common standards to govern it.

items.title: Turning Sub-Saharan Africa’s Cities Into Job Engines
items.desc: Cities and towns will be central to creating more and better jobs for Sub-Saharan Africa’s fast-growing population, simply because the region’s people and economic activity are increasingly concentrated there. But unlocking urbanization’s potential requires policy guidance and well-planned investment.

items.title: Why Are Indian Protesters Targeting the Electoral Commission?
items.desc: Following a “special intensive revision” that struck 130 million voters from the electoral rolls, India’s youth have mounted large-scale protests against the Election Commission. Given the convergence of protests with the formal political opposition, the Commission is unlikely to avoid accountability for mass disenfranchisement.

items.title: Why Aren’t We Investing More in Climate Adaptation?
items.desc: There are many proven ways to protect people and assets from extreme weather, and such measures often prevent economic losses worth many times their cost. But ensuring their implementation requires making them more affordable and creating innovative revenue mechanisms and financing structures.

items.title: Put the Ocean at the Center of COP31
items.desc: Last year’s UN Climate Change Conference in Belém, Brazil, put forests high on the climate agenda. This month’s UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, can do the same for the ocean, whose warming threatens not just food and energy security but global survival.

items.title: Who's Winning (and Who's Losing) The Ocean?
items.desc: Ahead of COP31, PS sat down with Peter Thomson, the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy for the Ocean, to discuss the logic of “blue” economic development. Watch as he warns of a “world on fire,” takes governments to task for kowtowing to the oil and gas industry, and explains how we can do better for future generations.

items.title: The Democrats’ Historic Duty
items.desc: While Democrats have good reason to celebrate their historic midterm victory, their current elation must quickly harden into determination. Fortunately, the field for new ideas, systemic and economic, in the US will be the most open it is likely to be for decades.

items.title: Dot-Com Lessons for the AI Bubble
items.desc: Anyone who lived through the internet boom and bust of the late 1990s and early 2000s should find the current AI investment cycle worryingly familiar. Heavy reliance on debt means that if investors decide to stop lending into the boom, a financial crisis will be inevitable—and far worse than the subprime-mortgage crisis in 2008.

items.title: China Is Defanging the Dollar, Not Dethroning It
items.desc: China offers Iran and Russia a way to circumvent US sanctions and continue doing business. But this comes at an elevated cost, because these countries are paid in onshore, non-convertible renminbi, which they must then convert into dollars using underground financial networks—tacitly reinforcing the greenback’s dominance.
